name: Sampling, Temperature and Decoding
intent: Understand how a model turns its scores for the next token into one chosen token, and what temperature, top-k and top-p do to the result.
scenario: The same prompt gives a safe, repeatable answer at temperature 0 and a lively but sometimes wrong one at temperature 1.5. A team wants to know which setting to use for invoice extraction and which for a brainstorming tool.
problem: A language model does not output a word. For every position it outputs a score for each token in its vocabulary, tens of thousands of numbers. Something must turn those scores into one token, and then repeat that for every token of the answer. Always taking the top score gives dull, repetitive text, and drawing at random from all of them lets in strange tokens. The decoding settings are how you choose between the two.

howItWorks.title: The model outputs scores for every token
howItWorks.text: At each position the model produces one raw score, a logit, for every token in the vocabulary. A higher score means the model finds that token a better continuation. The scores are not yet probabilities.

howItWorks.title: Temperature reshapes the probabilities
howItWorks.text: The scores are divided by the temperature and passed through a softmax, which turns them into probabilities that add up to 1. A temperature below 1 makes the distribution sharper, so the top token gains probability. Above 1 it flattens, so unlikely tokens gain. As the temperature approaches 0, the choice approaches always taking the top token.

howItWorks.title: Greedy decoding takes the top token
howItWorks.text: Always choosing the most likely token is deterministic and simple. For open-ended text it tends to produce repetitive, dull passages, one of the findings of the paper that introduced nucleus sampling. It suits tasks with one right answer, such as extraction.

howItWorks.title: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens
howItWorks.text: Top-k removes everything except the k most likely tokens and renormalises. The number is the same whatever the shape of the distribution: when the model is sure, k tokens still let unlikely ones in, and when it is unsure, k can cut good options.

howItWorks.title: Top-p keeps the smallest set that adds up to p
howItWorks.text: Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, sorts the tokens by probability and keeps the smallest set whose probabilities add up to at least p. The set adapts: a few tokens when the model is confident, many when it is not. The tail of unlikely tokens is cut off.

howItWorks.title: Draw one token, and repeat
howItWorks.text: A token is drawn at random from what is left, with the remaining probabilities renormalised, and added to the text. Then the model is run again for the next position. Even at temperature 0 results are only mostly repeatable in practice: when two tokens have nearly equal scores, tiny numerical differences from hardware or batching can change which one is on top.

pros: One setting moves a model between safe and varied output without retraining it
Low temperature gives stable, predictable answers for extraction and classification
Top-p adapts to how confident the model is at each step
The settings are free to change per request, so different features can use different values
cons: Higher temperature raises the chance of wrong or odd tokens, and one bad token can derail the rest of the answer
Temperature 0 is not a guarantee of identical output across runs, hardware or batching
The best values depend on the model and the task, so they have to be tested
No setting makes a model know facts it does not know, so they do not cure hallucination
whenToUse: You need repeatable output for extraction, classification or code: use a low temperature
You need variety for brainstorming or creative writing: raise the temperature and cut the tail with top-p
You are tuning a feature and need to explain why output changes between runs
whenNotToUse: Do not raise the temperature to make the model more accurate: it increases randomness, not knowledge
Do not rely on temperature 0 for exact repeatability in tests: allow for small differences
Do not tune temperature, top-k and top-p all at once without a way to measure the result
pitfalls: Assuming temperature 0 always gives the same answer
Setting a high temperature for a task with one correct answer, such as data extraction
Applying top-k and top-p without knowing the order they are applied in by your library
Judging a setting on a handful of examples instead of a set of cases that you can score

roles.label: Model
roles.description: Produces one raw score (a logit) for every token in the vocabulary.

roles.label: Temperature
roles.description: Divides the scores before the softmax: below 1 sharpens the probabilities, above 1 flattens them.

roles.label: Top-k and top-p
roles.description: Cut the unlikely tail so that only the plausible tokens can be drawn.

roles.label: Sampler
roles.description: Draws one token from what is left, adds it to the text and asks the model for the next one.

sources.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration

quiz.question: A team extracts invoice numbers and totals with a model and wants the same answer for the same invoice every time. Which is the best first step?
options: Raise the temperature, so that the model tries more possible answers and the right one appears
Use a higher top-k, so that more tokens are available for each position in the answer
Use a very low temperature (or greedy decoding), and validate the output against the invoice
Ask the model in the prompt to answer in a way that is always exactly the same
quiz.explanation: A low temperature makes the top token almost always the one chosen, which suits a task with one right answer. Because tiny numerical differences can still change results, the output should also be validated. A higher temperature or a larger top-k adds randomness, and a request in the prompt does not control the sampler.

quiz.question: A story-writing assistant produces repetitive, bland text at temperature 0. Which change is most likely to help without letting nonsense in?
options: Raise the temperature a little and use top-p to cut off the unlikely tail of tokens
Set top-k to 1, so that the model has only one option and cannot make mistakes
Set the temperature as high as possible, so that all tokens are equally likely
Repeat the prompt several times, so that the model sees how varied the answer should be
quiz.explanation: Always taking the top token tends to repeat itself in open-ended text. A moderate temperature adds variety, and top-p removes the very unlikely tokens that would produce nonsense. Top-k of 1 is the same as greedy decoding, and a very high temperature makes the tokens nearly equally likely, which gives noise.

quiz.question: Why is top-p often preferred to a fixed top-k such as 40?
options: Top-p is faster, because it removes the need for a softmax over the scores
Top-k does not work with a temperature, so top-p is the only option when temperature is used
Top-p always keeps exactly one token, which makes the output more consistent
The set of kept tokens adapts: few when the model is confident, more when it is not, while top-k keeps a fixed number
quiz.explanation: When the model is sure, 40 tokens let in many poor options, and when it is unsure, 40 may cut good ones. Top-p keeps the smallest set that adds up to p, so its size follows the shape of the distribution. Both work with temperature and both need the probabilities.
